title: Peace be with you (John 20:19–23)
hook: behind locked doors he breathes on them: receive the Holy Spirit

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary turned at her name and said Rabboni. Your line was I have seen the lord. Who did you tell about something good you'd seen? Day six hundred fifty-two.

It's the evening of that same Sunday. Mary has told them. They've heard the tomb is empty. And where are they? In a room with the doors locked. John says they're afraid of the authorities who had Jesus arrested. Think about that: the best news in the world has reached them, and they're still behind a bolted door, listening for footsteps on the stairs. Most of us know that room. The news can be good, and the fear can still be louder. And then, without a knock, he's standing among them.

His first words, in the King James Bible: "Peace be unto you." It's an everyday greeting, like the Hebrew shalom, the hello anyone might say coming through a door. But think about who's saying it, and to whom. These are the friends who ran, who hid, one of whom denied knowing him three times. He doesn't start with, where were you? He starts with peace. Then he shows them his hands and his side, the wounds still there. And John says: "Then were the disciples glad, when they saw the Lord." He says it again, peace be unto you, and gives them a job: "as my Father hath sent me, even so send I you." Then the strangest gesture in the passage: "he breathed on them, and saith unto them, Receive ye the Holy Ghost." The Greek verb for breathed on is a rare one. It's the same word the old Greek translation of Genesis uses when God breathes into the first human, and he becomes a living soul. So John may be telling us this is a new creation, a new beginning, starting in a locked room. Then he speaks about forgiving sins: whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven. Churches read that line in different ways. Catholic and Orthodox Christians see in it the authority given to the church to forgive sins in confession. Many Protestants hear it as the power given to every believer to proclaim forgiveness in Jesus's name. All of them hear forgiveness at the center of the very first evening.
screen: `AS THE FATHER SENT ME, I SEND YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: breathe out peace. Settle, and breathe. Notice your own locked room today: the worry you keep the door bolted on. Breathe in slowly. As you breathe out, let the word peace go out with your breath, toward that worry. Then toward someone who's let you down. Then toward someone you've let down. Peace, on the out-breath, each time. If you pray, you can receive his words as spoken to you: peace be unto you. If you don't, simply let your breath carry goodwill. The bell holds the time.
Peace be with you. The risen Jesus's first words to friends who had run away, spoken through a locked door.
Your line: peace be with you. Today, start one hard conversation with peace instead of with where were you. Day six hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: In many churches the minister greets the congregation with 'peace be with you' or 'the Lord be with you', and Catholic and Orthodox Christians link this passage with the sacrament of confession.

fork.setup: your friends ran away when you were arrested. now you're back, and they're hiding behind locked doors. what are your first words?
options: I forgive you, but you'll have to earn it.
fork.reveal: his first words are peace, then he shows them his wounds, then he sends them.

original.note: Greek: he breathed on, he breathed into. the same verb as Genesis 2:7 in the Septuagint.

trapdoor: what you thought: a polite greeting.
what it means: peace offered first to friends who ran, then a breath that gives the Spirit.
what a scholar hears: enephysesen, used in the Septuagint at Genesis 2:7 when God breathes life into the first human: a new creation in a locked room.

notes: 'For fear of the Jews' (20:19) is paraphrased as 'the authorities who had Jesus arrested'. Confirm.
emphysao: in the NT only at John 20:22; LXX Genesis 2:7 uses the same verb. Confirm.
Two readings of 20:23 given without ranking. Keeper should confirm fairness.
Reviewer softened: Jesus's spoken greeting was likely Aramaic (shlama), so shalom is now given as a comparison, not the exact word.
Pentecost (Acts 2) is a separate giving of the Spirit in Luke's account; the script doesn't harmonize them. Keeper may want a note.
